textbookText: 7.2 Newton’s Law of Gravitation
So far, we are observing the phenomenon described in
activity 7.1, where there is a gravitational interaction
between any two bodies, whether terrestrial or
celestial. From the study of the apple's fall, Newton
established the famous law known as Newton’s Law
of Gravitation. This law was announced by Newton in
1687 in his monumental work, 'Principia.'
According to this law, any two particles in the
universe attract each other with a force.
Fig 7.1: Gravitational force between two bodies
The force is directly proportional to the product of the masses of the bodies, and inversely
proportional to the square of the distance apart them.

i.e, F ∝ r2 m1 m2 ∴F = G 2 m1 m2 r Here, G is the universal gravitational constant. If m1=m2=1 kg and d=1m Then, F = G Hence, G represents the force of attraction between two bodies of unit masses when they are kept at a unit distance apart.
7.3 Acceleration due to Gravity

The acceleration produced on a body due to Earth’s gravity is called acceleration due to gravity. It is symbolized by 'g,' and its value is 9.8 ms-1 ². It is independent of the size and shape of the body.
A body thrown up is found to have its velocity decreased by 9.8 ms-1 each second, while for the falling body, it is found to be increased by the same value each second.
For a body of mass ‘m’ lying on the surface of the Earth, one writes-
GMm F = R2
M → mass of the Earth
R → radius of the Earth
From Newton’s Second Law of motion,
F = mg.
GMm ∴ mg = 2 R GM ⇒g= 2 R Since G and M are constants, g ∝ 1/R2
